Weekly Coaching · November 16–20, 2026

Seven red days, and the S&P 500 stopped on its 61.8% line.

The S&P 500 lost 8.6% this week and closed Friday at 6,910.39, 10 points above the 61.8% retracement of its whole spring-to-fall run. Nvidia beat its numbers on Tuesday and lost 23% by Friday. This is the honest review: what we called, what it cost, what we learned, and the plan for a short holiday week.

Your trade

All cash, nothing new logged

You told me Thursday you're all cash, and nothing new has come in since. Everything below is the paper record we grade ourselves on, not your account.

The miss first

My SPY call was wrong on day one

Last Sunday I locked in: up, the $744–745 floor holds, target $763. SPY broke that floor on Monday's close ($739.95) and finished the week at $689.81. Score: 0 of 3. I leaned on two Fib lines overlapping and ignored that the 14-day and 30-day averages had already turned down. Overlap makes a level louder; it doesn't make it stronger than the trend.

The other miss: the GOOGL put idea waited for a bounce to $280 that came Friday, but by then GOOGL was already through our target. It fell 10.3% without us.

What mattered this week

Seven things, in order of weight

  • Nvidia beat, then broke. Revenue $115.84B vs $109.1B expected on Tuesday; by Friday it was $125.53 (−14% on the day, −22.9% on the week) after Reuters reported SEC staff are reviewing possible accounting issues and the 10-Q was delayed.
  • The AI hardware complex went with it. The chip index fell 10.7% Friday with all 30 names down; SMH −17.8% on the week, BE −25.8%, CRDO −24.1%, DELL −19.3%.
  • The S&P 500 is in a correction. Seven straight losses (longest since Feb 2020), 10.7% under its Oct 6 record. The VIX closed near 38, its highest close since April 2025.
  • Bonds rallied, gold didn't. The 2-year fell 15.5bp Friday to 4.62%, the 10-year 13.8bp to 4.91%. Gold fell every day of the week, to about $3,515.
  • Factories slowed, prices didn't. Philly Fed 6.3 vs 20.6 expected, Empire 7.8 vs 17.6, industrial production −0.4%; Philly prices paid jumped to 58.2.
  • The Fed still leans to a hike. Minutes: "a couple" floated more than 25bp; futures price about 92% for a hike on Dec 9.
  • Anthropic listed. Priced $83, opened $111.50, closed Friday $88.91. Amazon and Alphabet traded as its proxies.

Top 3 actionable

  1. AMZN Dec 18 $225 put, on a 15-minute close under $244.50: the 15th test of your 2.0 and the 200-day failing. R:R 2.6 to 1 to your 1.618 ($229.47). Liquidity OK (OI 11,856, 2,016 traded, spread 8%). EXPENSIVE (1.56). Force: the AI-backer unwind.
  2. XOM Dec 18 $165 call, over $161.60 after a session holding your 1.618 ($159.09). R:R 1.65 to 1. FAIR (1.17). Liquidity: OI 6,240, 616 traded, but the closing spread was 23%; act only if it is under 10%. Force: XOM rose on a −3.7% day.
  3. GOOGL Dec 18 $250 put, on a bounce into $270–272 that fails. R:R 3.1 to 1. Liquidity OK (OI 12,628, 3,359 traded, spread 8%). EXPENSIVE (1.37). Force: the same AI-backer unwind; only one of AMZN or GOOGL can be taken (see the plays).

Read the panel as one picture: stocks down, yields down, gold down, the dollar flat. That's not an inflation scare (gold would rise) and not a dollar squeeze (the dollar would jump). It's people selling what they can, to raise cash, and buying Treasuries as the only thing left to hide in. That hits every crowded long on the list at once, which is why KO and XOM, the two names that rose Friday, are the only longs in tonight's plays.

What's going on

Four forces behind the week

1. The AI trade is being repriced for trust, not demand

What we see: Nvidia reported revenue of $115.84B against about $109.1B expected and guided the next quarter to about $130B, then fell 22.9% on the week. Why: Reuters reported Friday that SEC enforcement staff are reviewing possible accounting issues; the 10-Q is delayed "in the coming weeks" with a board-committee investigation. Receivables stretched to 64 days, the longest since 2022, and the disclosure questions involve a Singapore customer suspected of moving chips to China. A new Commerce rule requires licenses for 16nm-and-better chips sold to Chinese designers. Broadcom fell 12.2% on a survey saying Google cut 2027 TPU shipments by about a million units. My read: the market stopped paying for demand it can't verify. I'm fairly sure of the direction, not of the floor. What proves me wrong: Nvidia files the 10-Q with no restatement, and SMH gets back over its 200-day ($525). Names: NVDA, AMD, SMH, DELL (reports Tuesday), CRDO, VRT, BE, INTC, PLTR.

2. Forced selling, not a new opinion

What we see: gold fell every day while Treasuries rallied, on options-expiry Friday. Why: Goldman's CTA model had trigger levels at 7,657, 7,555 and 7,133 on the S&P; all three broke this week, which flips trend-following funds to sellers (Goldman estimated about $123bn of global selling over a month in a falling tape). Hedge funds were net sellers for a second week and their tech long/short ratio hit 1.50, the lowest since 2016. Meanwhile ordinary fund buyers kept coming: US equity funds took in $45.7bn in the week to Nov 18 (Lipper). My read: professionals are de-risking into a crowd that's still buying dips. That's how 7-day streaks happen. What proves me wrong: gold and stocks rising together again with the VIX back under 30. Names: everything; GLD and TLT most directly.

3. The bond market sees a slowdown; the Fed sees inflation

What we see: Philly Fed 6.3 vs 20.6 expected, Empire 7.8 vs 17.6, industrial production −0.4%. But Philly prices paid jumped to 58.2 from 43.2. The 2-year fell 15.5bp Friday and markets cut next March's hike pricing to 48bp from 59bp, yet still price about 92% for a December hike. Why: the minutes said "a couple" of officials floated a move bigger than 25bp; Governor Cook said Friday waiting risks falling "behind the curve". My read: the market now expects the Fed to hike into a slowdown, which is why long bonds rallied. That's good for TLT and bad for anything priced on distant growth. What proves me wrong: a hot October PCE on Wednesday sends yields back up. Names: TLT, IWM, KO.

4. The shopper is fine; the AI build-out is not

What we see: Walmart beat and raised its full-year EPS range to $2.84–2.89; its CEO called the consumer "resilient". Target comps rose 5.6% vs 3.8% expected; TJX raised its comp guide; October retail sales control +0.6% vs 0.4%. Why it matters: staples (XLP) fell 2.0% this week while tech (XLK) fell 12.5%. This is a sector sell-off, not a recession trade. What proves me wrong: a sharp drop in Tuesday's consumer confidence. Names: KO, AMZN's retail side, AAPL.

Post-mortems, scored (thesis · risk · process · clarity, 2 each)

  • NVDA $140 put, 7/8. The thesis (a failed bounce under your 0.5, then a new 52-week low) was right, and the stop at $148.80 was a real level. But the SEC report did most of the work in one session. Process lost a point: the entry came at the close and the strike was switched from $145 for budget. Lesson: when a news gap pays you, take it; don't count it as proof the setup works.
  • INTC $55 put, 6/8. Target ($51.51, the Nov 5 low) hit late Friday. Honest note: INTC traded $59.44 on Thursday, over the $57.20 stop line. It survived only because that stop was close-based. Under our new intraday stops it would have been a loss. One sample, but write it down.
  • AAPL $360 call, 5/8. A clean trend-continuation entry with a stop at the 14-day, taken in a market that had just lost its own 200-day. The stop did its job (−35%, not −80%). Proposal for you to confirm: no trend-continuation calls while the S&P 500 is under its 200-day.
  • Two ideas on names you removed. One call scored 2/8 (a thin contract we should have dropped a week earlier), one put 6/8 (right direction, retired before target). Net +$170.

What the filters saved and cost us

Saved: the NVDA $170 call and AMZN $280 call were cancelled before entry; both would have lost most of their value. Cost: we skipped SPY puts twice as over budget and EXPENSIVE, and withdrew HOOD and NOW puts as stretched. SPY fell another 5.7% from Thursday's skip, HOOD 20%, NOW 14%. The EXPENSIVE label is right about price but this week it kept us out of the biggest moves. I'm not changing the rule on one week, but I'm logging it.

Masters checklist

Six questions, answered honestly

  1. Druckenmiller, liquidity: the Fed is priced to hike Dec 9, the dollar is up 2.5% in a month, and the 2-year fell only because growth cracked. Liquidity is tightening. The live paper ideas are three puts: we lean with it.
  2. Griffin, sizing: the PLTR put now carries 49% of the paper risk to stops, over our 25% flag, because it ran the most. Total risk to stops is $1,817 against a $2,500 cap. If one more idea triggers, the PLTR put should give back the most.
  3. Tudor Jones, defense first: every idea had its stop and thesis-broken line from the start, and the AAPL, KO and XOM stops were honored. One gap: INTC's stop was breached intraday and only the old close rule saved it.
  4. Marks, the cycle: AAII bears fell to 42.2% from 51.4% while prices fell. Fund buyers added $45.7bn. The crowd is still buying dips; we are not. That's the right side of the cycle question, and the wrong side of a bounce.
  5. Simons, the data: no setup has 20 graded. Level failure puts are 2-0 and the best early read; trend continuation is 0-2.
  6. Price structure: your levels failed in order on PLTR, XOM, AMZN, NVDA, OXY and DAL. In each case the structure said downtrend before any indicator did. The one level that held all week was AMZN's 2.618, as a ceiling.

Hedge funds and flows

Fed and macro

A hike into a slowdown

The target range is 3.75–4.00%. The Nov 18 minutes said "a couple" of officials floated more than 25bp in December; Cook said Friday that waiting risks falling "behind the curve"; Waller called for "aggressive action". Futures price about 92% for a 25bp hike on Dec 9. The Fed goes quiet next week (blackout), so Wednesday's October PCE and the Beige Book are the only Fed-relevant news before the meeting.

For the plays: a hiking Fed helps the PLTR and BA paper puts and the AMZN and GOOGL put ideas. It hurts the XOM call idea (slower demand for oil) and does little to KO, which is a defensive hold either way.

Lesson of the week

Nine tickers, one trade

Correlation means things that move together. Friday, NVDA fell 14.0%, AMD 13.2%, BE 15.3%, CRDO 15.2%, DELL 11.0%, VRT 10.1%, ORCL 8.5% and INTC 8.0%. Different companies, one driver: the AI build-out. If you had five calls on five of them, you had one bet five times.

That's why the desk has a correlation gate: once three live ideas share a driver, a fourth is blocked unless it replaces one. Next week it matters: the PLTR paper put is an AI short, and the AMZN and GOOGL put ideas share the same driver. So only one of AMZN or GOOGL can be taken; whichever triggers first wins the slot.

Practice: next to each idea on your list, write the one force that would hurt it. If two ideas share a force, they are one idea.

Fib lesson of the week · retracement week

Strikes and targets: let the ladder pick the option

Last week's ask first: your S&P extension hasn't come in, so it stays open. Tonight's example is that same swing, measured as a retracement.

The anchors: the Mar 30 low, 6,316.91, and the Oct 6 record, 7,844.52. They're the start and end of the year's main trend, the swing every desk is measuring. Range: 1,527.61 points.

The math: high − range × ratio. 23.6% = 7,484.00 (lost Monday) · 38.2% = 7,260.97 (lost Thursday) · 50% = 7,080.72 (lost Friday) · 61.8% = 7,844.52 − 1,527.61 × 0.618 = 6,900.46 · 78.6% = 6,643.82.

What price did: Friday's low was 6,882.66, 18 points under the 61.8%; the close was 6,910.39, back above. That's a wick, not a break. The next close decides.

61.8% 6,900.46 · Friday low 6,882.66 · close 6,910.39 · 78.6% 6,643.82 · 50% 7,080.72

Turning it into a trade: the target picks the strike. On a 15-minute close under 6,880, the target is the 78.6% at 6,643.82, about SPY $663 (SPY trades near SPX ÷ 10.02). A put struck near the target ($660–665) gains most of its value right where you plan to sell it. Stop back over 6,960 (about SPY $695): 3.0 to 1. For the bounce, a close back over 7,080.72 (about SPY $707) targets the 50% as the first line of resistance, so a $705–710 call.

Then check the price tag: the SPY $650 put costs $1,081 with IV at 2.1× realized. The ladder says where; the option price says not now. Both answers count.
